claims.claim: Local O2 concentrations in C. elegans natural habitats vary and might serve to indicate the presence of bacterial food, pathogens or predators.
claims.source: In nature, C. elegans is found in association with anthropogenic soil habitats constituting complex environments rich in olfactory cues (Félix and Braendle, 2010; Félix and Duveau, 2012), in which local O2 concentrations vary and might serve to indicate the presence of bacterial food, pathogens or predators (Sexstone et al., 1985).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation and represents speculation about the ecological significance of oxygen variation.

claims.claim: In the laboratory, worms are fed on E. coli lawns, which generate steep O2 gradients ranging from atmospheric 21% down to 12% O2.
claims.source: In the laboratory, worms are fed on E. coli lawns, which generate steep O2 gradients ranging from atmospheric 21% down to 12% O2 (Gray et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work characterizing oxygen gradients in laboratory conditions.

claims.claim: A sudden decline in O2 levels activates BAG class O2 sensory neurons.
claims.source: A sudden decline in O2 levels activates BAG class O2 sensory neurons (Zimmer et al., 2009), and during navigation of spatial O2 gradients, animals accumulate at intermediate concentrations (Cheung et al., 2005; Gray et al., 2004; Zimmer et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work characterizing BAG neuron responses.

claims.claim: During navigation of spatial O2 gradients, animals accumulate at intermediate concentrations.
claims.source: A sudden decline in O2 levels activates BAG class O2 sensory neurons (Zimmer et al., 2009), and during navigation of spatial O2 gradients, animals accumulate at intermediate concentrations (Cheung et al., 2005; Gray et al., 2004; Zimmer et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature describing O2 chemotaxis behavior.

claims.claim: Interneuron circuits that are involved in locomotory responses to changes in ambient O2 and that communicate with O2 sensory neurons have been partially described.
claims.source: Interneuron circuits that are involved in locomotory responses to changes in ambient O2 and that communicate with O2 sensory neurons have been partially described (Busch et al., 2012; Kato et al., 2015; Laurent et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature describing interneuron circuits involved in oxygen responses.

claims.claim: The navigational strategies used during O2 chemotaxis are uncharacterized.
claims.source: However, the navigational strategies used during O2 chemotaxis are uncharacterized.
claims.evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claims.claim: An immediate drop from atmospheric 21% to 10% O2 evoked a variety of behavioral changes, including transient reduction of locomotion speed and concomitant up-regulation of reversals and omega turns.
claims.source: An immediate drop from atmospheric 21% to 10% O2 (O2 downshift) evoked a variety of behavioral changes, including transient reduction of locomotion speed and concomitant up-regulation of reversals and omega turns as previously described (Zimmer et al., 2009) (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and is consistent with previously published results.

claims.claim: O2 downshift caused up-regulation of shallow turning maneuvers during forward movement, evident as increased curvature of the animals' locomotion trajectories.
claims.source: In addition, we observed up-regulation of shallow turning maneuvers during forward movement, evident as increased curvature of the animals' locomotion trajectories (track curvature) (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: The compound effect of behavioral changes upon O2 downshift was a drastic reduction in the spatial displacement of worms during the first three minutes.
claims.source: The compound effect of these behavioral changes was a drastic reduction in the spatial displacement of worms during the first three minutes upon O2 downshift (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: A sudden drop in environmental O2 concentrations evoked a change in the locomotion strategy switching from predominantly forward crawling to a mixture of reduced crawling and increased reorientations, i.e. from LDT to O2-induced ARS.
claims.source: Thus, a sudden drop in environmental O2 concentrations evoked a change in the locomotion strategy switching from predominantly forward crawling to a mixture of reduced crawling and increased reorientations, i.e. from LDT to O2-induced ARS (see also Video 1 and Video 2 upper left panel).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data shown in Figure 1 and Videos 1-2.

claims.claim: This interpretation is in accordance with previous literature classifying similar behavioral strategy changes in the context of removal from food.
claims.source: This interpretation is in accordance with previous literature classifying similar behavioral strategy changes in the context of removal from food (Calhoun et al., 2015; Gray et al., 2005; Hills et al., 2004; Peliti et al., 2013; Tsalik and Hobert, 2003; Wakabayashi et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature describing similar behavioral changes.

claims.claim: The changes in behavioral parameters all depended on an O2 chemosensory neuron pair, termed BAG.
claims.source: The changes in behavioral parameters all depended on an O2 chemosensory neuron pair, termed BAG, which is activated upon O2 downshift (Zimmer et al., 2009) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Upon O2 downshift, animals tended to stop forward locomotion and adopted complex and variable postures, unlike the more regular sinusoid-like postures associated with LDT.
claims.source: Upon O2 downshift, animals tended to stop forward locomotion and adopted complex and variable postures, unlike the more regular sinusoid-like postures associated with LDT (Figure 1D,E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by visual observations shown in Figure 1D,E.

claims.claim: LDT was associated with long stretches of regular and coherent body posture patterns, while O2-induced ARS after O2 downshift exhibited variability in the amplitude, direction and frequency of body postural changes.
claims.source: LDT was associated with long stretches of regular and coherent body posture patterns, while O2-induced ARS after O2 downshift exhibited variability in the amplitude, direction and frequency of body postural changes (Figure 1G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by posture kymograph data shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: Shallow turns, slowing bouts, reversals and omega turns occurred sparsely during LDT; however, during O2-induced ARS these behaviors were up-regulated 2-4-fold.
claims.source: Note that shallow turns, slowing bouts, reversals and omega turns also occurred sparsely during LDT; however, during O2-induced ARS these behaviors were up-regulated 2-4-fold (compare pre- with post- stimulus period in all panels of Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative comparisons of behavioral parameters shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Principal components analysis (PCA) calculates the eigenvectors (termed eigenworms, EWs) of the covariance matrix of inter-segment angles observed over many posture time series.
claims.source: Briefly, in this approach, principal components analysis (PCA) (Jolliffe, 2002) calculates the eigenvectors (termed eigenworms, EWs) of the covariance matrix of inter-segment angles observed over many posture time series (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This describes the mathematical method used, with a citation to the PCA methodology and reference to Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Linear combinations of the first four EWs account for the gross majority (>85%) of the observed postural variance.
claims.source: EW's are a set of representative worm postures (as defined by a vector of inter-segment angles), in descending order of explanatory power; i.e. each EW contributes a certain amount of postural variance and linear combinations of the first four EWs account for the gross majority (>85%) of the observed postural variance (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Despite the strong effect of O2 downshift on the animals' postures, the respective underlying EWs were nearly identical.
claims.source: We found that despite the strong effect of O2 downshift on the animals' postures, the respective underlying EWs were nearly identical (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison of eigenworms calculated from pre- and post-stimulus data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The percentage of total variance explained by EW1 and EW2 decreased whereas the percentage of total variance explained by lower-order EWs increased after O2 downshift.
claims.source: However, the relative contributions of each EW changed: the percentage of total variance explained by EW1 and EW2 decreased whereas the percentage of total variance explained by lower-order EWs increased (e.g. EW3-6, Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The different postures observed during LDT versus O2-induced ARS can be described by linear combinations of the same elementary shapes, the relative weights of which are modulated upon stimulation.
claims.source: Thus, the different postures observed during LDT versus O2-induced ARS can be described by linear combinations of the same elementary shapes, the relative weights of which are modulated upon stimulation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the eigenworm analysis data presented in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The combination of EW1 and 2 corresponds to the regular undulatory movements along the worm's body, which generates forward and backward crawling.
claims.source: The combination of EW1 and 2 corresponds to the regular undulatory movements along the worm's body, which generates forward and backward crawling (Stephens et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work characterizing the meaning of the first two eigenworms.

claims.claim: Strong transients in the residual time series (turning mode) coincided with shallow turns as well as with highly bent omega turns.
claims.source: Subtracting the undulation mode from the full body posture time series, which is equivalent to reconstructing posture time series based on all remaining EWs 3–24, revealed a strikingly organized residual mode. Strong transients in the residual time series coincided with shallow turns as well as with highly bent omega turns (see Figure 2C for examples); we thus termed this time series the 'turning mode'.
claims.evidence: This is supported by visual analysis of posture kymographs shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: The turning mode was qualitatively different in comparison to the undulation mode: the head moved in anti-phase with the tail and in phase with the mid-body whereas the undulation mode was generated by anti-phase undulations of head and mid-body and in phase undulation of head and tail.
claims.source: The turning mode was qualitatively different in comparison to the undulation mode: the head moved in anti-phase with the tail and in phase with the mid-body whereas the undulation mode was generated by anti-phase undulations of head and mid-body and in phase undulation of head and tail.
claims.evidence: This describes the qualitative characteristics of the two modes based on analysis of body segment movements.

claims.claim: The undulation mode and turning mode were not independent as they were often phase-locked: signal cross-correlation analysis showed that the onset of turning movements lagged on average ~0.6 s behind the undulation mode.
claims.source: The undulation mode and turning mode were not independent as they were often phase-locked: signal cross-correlation analysis showed that the onset of turning movements lagged on average ~0.6 s behind the undulation mode (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,F.

claims.claim: The diverse and complex postures observed in worms were obtained by simple linear addition of undulation and turning shapes.
claims.source: The diverse and complex postures observed in worms were obtained by simple linear addition of undulation and turning shapes (Figure 2D; Video 2).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by reconstructed worm shapes shown in Figure 2D and Video 2.

claims.claim: Apparently complex postures of C. elegans can be linearly composed out of simpler elementary shapes, which constitute behaviorally relevant motor patterns of the worm: the undulation mode describes regular forward and backward crawling, onto which the turning mode imposes turning movements.
claims.source: In conclusion, apparently complex postures of C. elegans can be linearly composed out of simpler elementary shapes, which constitute behaviorally relevant motor patterns of the worm: the undulation mode describes regular forward and backward crawling, onto which the turning mode imposes turning movements.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the eigenworm decomposition analysis presented in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Biomechanical calculations indicate that both body bending amplitude and frequency synergistically generate thrust against the substrate thereby contributing to the animals' locomotion speed.
claims.source: Biomechanical calculations indicate that both body bending amplitude and frequency synergistically generate thrust against the substrate thereby contributing to the animals' locomotion speed (Gray, 1953).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous biomechanical work.

claims.claim: High signals in turning amplitude consistently coincided with regions of high track curvature, i.e. events when animals adjusted their heading direction.
claims.source: High signals in turning amplitude consistently coincided with regions of high track curvature, i.e. events when animals adjusted their heading direction (see Figure 3A for examples); track curvature was a graded function of turning amplitude (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by trajectory analysis shown in Figure 3A and quantitative analysis in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Track curvature was a graded function of turning amplitude.
claims.source: High signals in turning amplitude consistently coincided with regions of high track curvature, i.e. events when animals adjusted their heading direction (see Figure 3A for examples); track curvature was a graded function of turning amplitude (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Turning amplitude and undulation amplitude exhibited a graded inverse relationship to each other.
claims.source: Turning amplitude and undulation amplitude exhibited a graded inverse relationship to each other (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Undulation frequency exhibited a tight linear relationship with translational locomotion speed.
claims.source: As expected, undulation frequency exhibited a tight linear relationship with translational locomotion speed (Figure 3D) (See also reference [Stephens et al., 2008]).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3D and is consistent with previous work.

claims.claim: Directional changes during forward movement were associated with slow locomotion: there was an inverse relationship between undulation frequency and centroid track curvature.
claims.source: We found that directional changes during forward movement were associated with slow locomotion: there was an inverse relationship between undulation frequency and centroid track curvature (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: High undulation amplitude was associated with fast locomotion (high undulation frequency) whereas high turning amplitude was associated with slow, low-frequency locomotion.
claims.source: High undulation amplitude was associated with fast locomotion (high undulation frequency) whereas high turning amplitude was associated with slow, low-frequency locomotion (Figures 3F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: All relationships between turning amplitude, undulation amplitude, undulation frequency, speed, and track curvature were preserved during both pre- and post-stimulus periods.
claims.source: All relationships described were preserved during both pre- and post- stimulus periods (Figure 3B–F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison of data from pre- and post-stimulus periods shown in Figure 3B-F.

claims.claim: During turning maneuvers, animals reduce the amplitude and speed of undulation motions, leading to slow locomotion.
claims.source: In conclusion, turning amplitude, undulation amplitude and undulation frequency are coupled: during turning maneuvers, animals reduce the amplitude and speed of undulation motions, leading to slow locomotion.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the quantitative relationships shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: During periods of fast locomotion turning maneuvers are suppressed.
claims.source: Contrarily during periods of fast locomotion turning maneuvers are suppressed.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the inverse relationship between turning amplitude and locomotion speed shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Under the experimental conditions used, the coupling of motor parameters is a robust property of worm locomotion during both spontaneous and stimulus-evoked behaviors.
claims.source: Under our experimental conditions, the coupling of these motor parameters is a robust property of worm locomotion during both spontaneous and stimulus-evoked behaviors.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that relationships between motor parameters are preserved across different behavioral contexts.

claims.claim: Upon stimulus onset, the mean amplitudes of turning and undulation modes were abruptly up- or down-regulated, respectively, and gradually returned to baseline within three minutes.
claims.source: Upon stimulus onset, the mean amplitudes were abruptly up- or down-regulated, respectively, and gradually returned to baseline within three minutes (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by time course data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Total body amplitude changed upon stimulation with a biphasic response profile, i.e. initial suppression followed by transient up-regulation.
claims.source: For comparison, we calculated the time course of total body amplitude, which changed upon stimulation with a biphasic response profile, i.e. initial suppression followed by transient up-regulation (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by time course data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: A gradual O2 ramp from 21% to 4% O2 caused a subtle change in mean total body amplitude but stronger and gradual reciprocal changes in mean undulation and turning amplitudes.
claims.source: To test this hypothesis, we stimulated the animals with a temporal oxygen ramp ranging from atmospheric 21% to 4% O2 (-0.01%/s). This protocol caused a subtle change in mean total body amplitude but stronger and gradual reciprocal changes in mean undulation and turning amplitudes (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by time course data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The skew of turning amplitude distribution functions gradually increased towards higher levels during the oxygen ramp, without showing bimodality.
claims.source: We then plotted the fraction of postures with a given turning amplitude as distribution functions during subsequent time segments of the ramp. We did not observe bimodality but instead that the skew of these distributions gradually increased towards higher levels (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by distribution analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Animals were able to gradually adjust turning and undulation motions within a wide continuous range.
claims.source: Thus, animals were able to gradually adjust turning and undulation motions within a wide continuous range, as further revealed in a two-dimensional density plot of turning amplitude against undulation frequency (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by 2D density plot analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Oxygen stimulation results in a shift in the contributions of undulation and turning motor patterns.
claims.source: In summary, oxygen stimulation results in a shift in the contributions of undulation and turning motor patterns.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Animals display control of the strength of undulation and turning motions in response to both abruptly and gradually changing environments.
claims.source: Animals display control of the strength of undulation and turning motions in response to both abruptly and gradually changing environments.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 4.

claims.claim: LDT and O2-induced ARS behaviors appear to lie on a continuum of behavioral mode compositions.
claims.source: LDT and O2-induced ARS behaviors appear to lie on a continuum of behavioral mode compositions.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the gradual nature of behavioral changes observed in response to oxygen stimuli.

claims.claim: flp-1 mutants have been reported to exhibit elevated body curvature and locomotion speed.
claims.source: flp-1 mutants have been reported to exhibit elevated body curvature and locomotion speed (Chang et al., 2015; Nelson et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature describing flp-1 mutant phenotypes.

claims.claim: NLP-12 neuropeptides have been reported to be exclusively released from the proprioceptive interneuron DVA.
claims.source: NLP-12 neuropeptides have been reported to be exclusively released from the proprioceptive interneuron DVA; interfering with the DVA/NLP-12 system leads to decreased body curvature and locomotion speed (Bhattacharya et al., 2014; Garrison et al., 2012; Hu et al., 2011; Janssen et al., 2008; Li et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature describing NLP-12 expression and function.

claims.claim: Interfering with the DVA/NLP-12 system leads to decreased body curvature and locomotion speed.
claims.source: NLP-12 neuropeptides have been reported to be exclusively released from the proprioceptive interneuron DVA; interfering with the DVA/NLP-12 system leads to decreased body curvature and locomotion speed (Bhattacharya et al., 2014; Garrison et al., 2012; Hu et al., 2011; Janssen et al., 2008; Li et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature describing DVA/NLP-12 function.

claims.claim: All previously reported phenotypes of flp-1 and nlp-12 mutants, DVA ablated animals, and transgenic nlp-12 rescue strains could be recapitulated in 1 hr fasted worms.
claims.source: We assayed flp-1 and nlp-12 mutants, DVA ablated (DVA-) animals, as well as transgenic nlp-12 rescue strains in DVA, and found that all phenotypes could be recapitulated in 1 hr fasted worms (Figure 5A,B; Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5A,B and 6A.

claims.claim: flp-1 expression in the single ventral ganglion interneuron class AVK is sufficient to restore a wild type phenotype.
claims.source: We found that flp-1 expression in the single ventral ganglion interneuron class AVK, which we observed to be the neuron class with strongest expression, is sufficient to restore a wild type phenotype (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: AVK ablation caused enhanced body posture amplitude similar to flp-1 mutants.
claims.source: We generated AVK- animals, which caused enhanced body posture amplitude similar to flp-1 mutants (Figure 5A,B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claims.claim: flp-1;nlp-12 double mutants as well as AVK-;DVA- animals exhibited intermediate total body amplitude similar to wild type levels, indicating an antagonism between both systems.
claims.source: flp-1;nlp-12 double mutants as well as AVK-;DVA- animals exhibited intermediate total body amplitude similar to wild type levels, indicating an antagonism between both systems (Figure 5A,B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A,B and represents an inference about the relationship between the two systems.

claims.claim: Interfering with AVK/FLP-1 function increased undulation amplitude, while interfering with DVA/NLP-12 decreased undulation amplitude.
claims.source: The decomposition revealed that a large proportion of altered body posture across all phenotypes could be explained by a corresponding effect on undulation amplitude. Interfering with AVK/FLP-1 function increased undulation amplitude, while interfering with DVA/NLP-12 decreased undulation amplitude . flp-1;nlp-12 double mutants exhibited intermediate phenotypes (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by eigenworm decomposition analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: All genotypes except flp-1;nlp-12 double mutants and DVA- animals showed an increase in turning amplitude, which was especially strong for flp-1 mutants and animals lacking AVK.
claims.source: In addition, all genotypes except flp-1;nlp-12 double mutants and DVA- animals showed an increase in turning amplitude, which was especially strong for flp-1 mutants and animals lacking AVK (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: To a large extent the postures of mutants and manipulated strains reflected postures that were exhibited, however less frequently, by wild type animals.
claims.source: A comparison of 2D probability density distributions of undulation vs. turning mode revealed that to a large extent the postures of mutants and manipulated strains reflected postures that were exhibited, however less frequently, by wild type animals (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by 2D density distribution analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: All analyzed mutant and cell ablation strains were compromised in regulating undulation and turning mode in response to O2 downshift.
claims.source: Besides their effects on worm postures at constant atmospheric O2 levels, all analyzed mutant and cell ablation strains were compromised in regulating undulation and turning mode in response to O2 downshift.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement about the stimulus-evoked behavioral defects observed across multiple genotypes.

claims.claim: The strongest defects in stimulus-evoked postural changes were seen in strains lacking AVK neurons, as well as in flp-1;nlp-12 double mutants.
claims.source: The strongest defects in stimulus-evoked postural changes were seen in strains lacking AVK neurons, as well as in flp-1;nlp-12 double mutants (Figure 5E–G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of stimulus-evoked changes shown in Figure 5E-G.

claims.claim: The DVA/NLP-12 and AVK/FLP-1 systems were both implicated in controlling locomotion speed.
claims.source: The DVA/NLP-12 and AVK/FLP-1 systems were both implicated in controlling locomotion speed (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by locomotion speed analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Cell-specific expression of nlp-12 in DVA and flp-1 in AVK partially restored the respective phenotypes.
claims.source: Cell-specific expression of nlp-12 in DVA and flp-1 in AVK partially restored the respective phenotypes, confirming these cells as important release sites for the respective neuropeptides (Figure 6A–F; Figure 5—figure supplement 2C,E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 6A-F and Figure 5—figure supplement 2C,E.

claims.claim: In the O2 ramp paradigm, flp-1;nlp-12 double mutant animals' modulation of undulation and turning amplitudes was largely compromised.
claims.source: However, we hypothesized that if the neuropeptides were part of a control system of worm postures, the double mutants should lack control over the composition of behavioral modes. Indeed, in the ramp paradigm the mutant animals' modulation of undulation and turning amplitudes was largely compromised (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by oxygen ramp experiment data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The phenotype of flp-1;nlp-12 double mutants in the ramp paradigm could be rescued by cell-specific expression of nlp-12 in DVA and flp-1 in AVK.
claims.source: This phenotype could be rescued by cell-specific expression of nlp-12 in DVA and flp-1 in AVK (Figure 6G–H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 6G-H.

claims.claim: Control of the composition of undulation and turning modes can be partially dissected at the genetic and single neuron level.
claims.source: In conclusion, control of the composition of undulation and turning modes can be partially dissected at the genetic and single neuron level.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the genetic and cellular manipulation experiments presented in Figures 5-6.

claims.claim: The DVA/NLP-12 and AVK/FLP-1 systems are required for normal body posture during LDT in constant environmental conditions as well as for the differential fine control of undulation and turning motions in response to both abruptly and smoothly changing environments.
claims.source: The DVA/NLP-12 and AVK/FLP-1 systems are required for normal body posture during LDT in constant environmental conditions as well as for the differential fine control of undulation and turning motions in response to both abruptly and smoothly changing environments.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the genetic and cellular manipulation experiments presented in Figures 5-6.

claims.claim: Decomposition of posture into undulation and turning modes is not only a useful quantitative description of behavior, but these motor patterns are under differential neural control.
claims.source: Our data suggest that decomposition of posture into undulation and turning modes is not only a useful quantitative description of behavior, but that these motor patterns are under differential neural control.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that genetic manipulations differentially affect the two motor modes.

claims.claim: AVK Ca2+ signals in average decreased upon O2 downshift in freely moving animals.
claims.source: We observed frequent Ca2+ transients of varying magnitude, which were associated with changes in the animal's locomotion speed. Consistent with this observation, AVK Ca2+ signals in average decreased upon O2 downshift (Figure 7B–C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7B-C.

claims.claim: AVK activity did not show O2 downshift-evoked changes in immobilized animals.
claims.source: When measuring AVK activity in immobilized animals, we did not detect O2 downshift-evoked activity changes (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data from immobilized animals shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: In freely moving animals, AVK activity positively correlated with locomotion speed.
claims.source: In freely moving animals, we found that AVK activity positively correlated with locomotion speed (Figure 7D), but unlike previously reported speed-encoding interneurons, which exclusively encode either forward or reverse locomotion speed (Kato et al., 2015; Li et al., 2014), AVK correlated with speed during both forward and reverse movement (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7D-E.

claims.claim: Unlike previously reported speed-encoding interneurons, which exclusively encode either forward or reverse locomotion speed, AVK correlated with speed during both forward and reverse movement.
claims.source: In freely moving animals, we found that AVK activity positively correlated with locomotion speed (Figure 7D), but unlike previously reported speed-encoding interneurons, which exclusively encode either forward or reverse locomotion speed (Kato et al., 2015; Li et al., 2014), AVK correlated with speed during both forward and reverse movement (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7E and comparison with previous literature.

claims.claim: AVK activity negatively correlated with turning amplitude during forward movement.
claims.source: Consistent with our findings that speed and turning motions were reciprocally regulated, AVK activity negatively correlated with turning amplitude during forward movement (Figure 7F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7F.

claims.claim: The relationship of AVK activity with behavioral output was unchanged when comparing pre- and post-stimulus periods.
claims.source: The relationship of AVK activity with behavioral output was unchanged when comparing pre- and post-stimulus periods (Figure 7G–H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis comparing pre- and post-stimulus periods shown in Figure 7G-H.

claims.claim: Elevated AVK neuronal activity reflects high locomotion speed and low turning amplitude, thus corresponding to aspects of motion rather than to sensory inputs.
claims.source: In summary, elevated AVK neuronal activity reflects high locomotion speed and low turning amplitude, thus corresponding to aspects of motion rather than to sensory inputs; similar observations have been made for many interneurons in C. elegans (Kato et al., 2015; Larsch et al., 2013; Laurent et al., 2015; Li et al., 2014; Luo et al., 2014b).
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the AVK calcium imaging data, with citations to similar findings in other interneurons.

claims.claim: The neural activity of AVK is consistent with the behavioral phenotypes of AVK- animals, which exhibit reduced locomotion speed and strong up-regulation of turning maneuvers.
claims.source: The neural activity is consistent with the behavioral phenotypes of AVK- animals, which exhibit reduced locomotion speed (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B) and strong up-regulation of turning maneuvers (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This is an inference connecting the neural activity data with the behavioral phenotype data.

claims.claim: AVK activity promotes locomotion speed and suppresses turning.
claims.source: Taken together, these results suggest that AVK activity promotes locomotion speed and suppresses turning.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation between AVK activity and behavioral parameters.

claims.claim: AVK can influence locomotion speed and turning suppression only in the context of feedback from the motor system.
claims.source: However, since AVK activity changes are low in immobilized worms we propose that AVK can influence these functions only in the context of feedback from the motor system.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that AVK activity changes are reduced in immobilized animals.

claims.claim: DVA Ca2+ signals increased on average upon O2 downshift in freely moving animals.
claims.source: DVA Ca2+ signals increased on average upon O2 downshift (Figure 8B,C upper panel, see Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,B for motion artifact controls).

results.result: C. elegans locomotion can be decomposed into two distinct motor modes using eigenworm analysis: an undulation mode (EW1-2) corresponding to regular forward/backward crawling, and a turning mode (EW3-24) corresponding to directional changes. These modes are linearly additive and account for >85% of postural variance, with their relative contributions changing upon O2 stimulation despite the underlying eigenworms remaining nearly identical.
results.evaluation: The eigenworm decomposition is rigorously demonstrated with PCA analysis (C32-C33), showing that the same eigenworm basis describes both LDT and ARS behaviors with only the relative weights changing (C34-C36). The linear additivity of the two modes is convincingly shown through reconstruction (C41-C42), and the phase-locking relationship is quantified via cross-correlation (C40). The mathematical approach is sound and well-validated.

results.result: An immediate drop from 21% to 10% O2 evokes a behavioral shift from long-distance traveling (LDT) to area-restricted search (ARS), characterized by reduced locomotion speed, increased track curvature, up-regulation of reversals and omega turns (2-4-fold), and adoption of complex variable postures. This response depends on BAG O2 sensory neurons.
results.evaluation: The behavioral changes are well-documented with quantitative data (C23-C25, C31) and appropriate controls showing BAG-dependence (C28). The characterization as a shift from LDT to ARS is supported by comparison with previous literature (C27). Sample sizes are adequate (n=36 assays) and the temporal dynamics are clearly shown. The only minor limitation is that BAG-ablated animals also lack ASG neurons, which could be a confound.

results.result: Turning amplitude, undulation amplitude, and undulation frequency exhibit lawful reciprocal relationships: turning amplitude inversely correlates with undulation amplitude and frequency, while undulation frequency positively correlates with locomotion speed. These relationships are preserved across both spontaneous and stimulus-evoked behaviors, indicating a fundamental tradeoff between efficient locomotion and flexible turning.
results.evaluation: The quantitative relationships are thoroughly characterized with appropriate binning and statistical analysis (C44-C49). The preservation of these relationships across different behavioral contexts (C50) strengthens the conclusion that this represents a fundamental constraint. The correlation between undulation frequency and speed is consistent with prior work (C47), providing external validation. The graded nature of these relationships is clearly demonstrated.

results.result: Animals can gradually adjust undulation and turning mode amplitudes in response to both abrupt O2 downshifts and gradual O2 ramps, demonstrating continuous control rather than discrete behavioral switching. During gradual O2 changes, turning amplitude distributions shift gradually without bimodality, indicating that LDT and ARS lie on a behavioral continuum.
results.evaluation: The gradual control is convincingly demonstrated through both step and ramp stimuli (C54, C56). The absence of bimodality in turning amplitude distributions (C57) and the 2D density plots (C58) provide strong evidence against discrete behavioral states. The biphasic response of total body amplitude (C55) contrasts with the monophasic responses of the decomposed modes, validating the utility of the eigenworm approach.

results.result: The AVK/FLP-1 and DVA/NLP-12 neuropeptide systems antagonistically control undulation and turning modes. AVK/FLP-1 suppresses both undulation and turning amplitude, while DVA/NLP-12 promotes undulation amplitude. Cell-specific rescue experiments confirm AVK and DVA as the relevant release sites, and double mutants show that these systems are required for stimulus-evoked postural control.
results.evaluation: The genetic dissection is thorough with appropriate mutants, cell ablations, and cell-specific rescues (C65-C67, C75). The antagonistic relationship is demonstrated by the intermediate phenotype of double mutants (C68). The eigenworm decomposition reveals differential effects on the two motor modes (C69-C70), supporting the claim of differential neural control (C80). The strongest defects in stimulus-evoked responses occur in AVK- and double mutants (C72-C73), confirming functional relevance.

results.result: flp-1;nlp-12 double mutants show compromised modulation of undulation and turning amplitudes during gradual O2 ramps, a phenotype that can be rescued by cell-specific expression of the neuropeptides in AVK and DVA, demonstrating that these systems are required for fine behavioral control in gradually changing environments.
results.evaluation: The ramp paradigm provides a sensitive test of graded behavioral control (C76), and the successful rescue (C77) confirms the specificity of the genetic manipulation. This result is particularly important because the double mutants have near-normal baseline behavior, isolating the deficit to stimulus-evoked control. The experimental design appropriately tests the hypothesis that the neuropeptides are part of a control system.

results.result: AVK neuronal activity positively correlates with locomotion speed during both forward and reverse movement and negatively correlates with turning amplitude. AVK activity decreases upon O2 downshift in freely moving but not immobilized animals, suggesting AVK functions in the context of motor feedback to promote speed and suppress turning.
results.evaluation: The calcium imaging data are well-controlled with mCherry ratiometric correction and GFP controls (C81-C82). The correlations with behavior are quantified and consistent across pre- and post-stimulus periods (C83-C86). The bidirectional speed encoding (C84) is a novel finding. The lack of response in immobilized animals (C82) supports the motor feedback hypothesis (C90), though this remains somewhat speculative. The consistency with AVK- behavioral phenotypes (C88) strengthens the interpretation.

results.result: DVA neuronal activity increases upon O2 downshift and correlates with multiple behavioral features including reversals, pausing, and transient increases in undulation amplitude with reciprocal decreases in turning amplitude. The O2-evoked DVA response is abolished when restricting analysis to forward locomotion only, indicating DVA activity primarily reflects behavioral state changes rather than direct sensory encoding.
results.evaluation: The calcium imaging is properly controlled (C91) and the multiple behavioral correlates are systematically characterized (C92-C93, C96). The peak-triggered average analysis (C96) is an appropriate method for detecting transient relationships. The lack of global correlation with forward locomotion parameters (C95) combined with the loss of O2-evoked response when excluding reversals/pauses (C94) supports the interpretation that DVA encodes behavioral state transitions. The failure to detect a signal with total body amplitude (C97) validates the eigenworm approach.

results.result: Wild-type C. elegans perform O2 chemotaxis toward ~16% O2 using multiple navigational strategies: weathervaning (curving bias strongest at 90° bearing), biased random walk (modulation of reversal rates), and bearing-dependent modulation of speed and turning amplitude, with all strategies showing graded responses as a function of heading direction.
results.evaluation: The chemotaxis behavior is thoroughly characterized with appropriate controls (C101) and multiple complementary metrics (C102-C105). The weathervaning analysis properly accounts for bearing angle (C102), and the gradual modulation of multiple parameters (C103-C105) demonstrates the sophistication of the navigational strategy. The sample size (n=53 assays) is adequate. The preferred O2 concentration differs from previous studies, but this is explained by different experimental conditions (1 hr vs longer starvation, no hypoxia).

results.result: flp-1;nlp-12 double mutants show specific defects in O2 chemotaxis: compromised weathervaning and impaired bearing-dependent modulation of speed and turning, while retaining the ability to modulate reversal rates. This demonstrates that the AVK/FLP-1 and DVA/NLP-12 systems are specifically required for weathervaning and ARS-like behavior modulation but not for the biased random walk strategy.
results.evaluation: The chemotaxis defects are well-characterized with appropriate quantification (C109-C110, C113, C115). The selective preservation of reversal rate modulation (C114) while other strategies are impaired (C113, C115) demonstrates specificity. The similar defects in single mutants (C111) support the involvement of both neuropeptide systems. The focus on double mutants is justified because single mutants show confounding baseline distribution differences (C112). The conclusion that fine-tuned control is essential for navigation (C116) is well-supported.

results.result: The combination of elementary motor patterns (undulation and turning modes) enables flexible adjustment of locomotion strategy along a continuum from LDT to ARS. Neuromodulatory peptidergic circuits gradually adjust these motor parameters while enforcing reciprocal relationships, allowing animals to balance the tradeoff between efficient displacement and flexible exploration according to instantaneous needs.
results.evaluation: This integrative conclusion is well-supported by the combined evidence from behavioral decomposition (C2, C42), gradual control (C3, C60-C61), neural mechanisms (C4, C79, C124), and functional validation through chemotaxis (C5, C118). The concept of a tradeoff between stereotypy and flexibility (C1, C126) is demonstrated through the reciprocal relationships between motor parameters (C46, C51-C52). The claim that behaviors lie on a continuum (C123) is supported by the absence of bimodality (C57) and gradual modulation (C58).

results.result: Background context establishing that animals use distinct foraging strategies (ARS vs LDT), that C. elegans exhibits similar behavioral strategies in response to food removal, that multiple chemotaxis strategies exist, and that C. elegans responds to O2 gradients in its natural habitat. The navigational strategies during O2 chemotaxis were previously uncharacterized.
results.evaluation: These claims establish the conceptual framework and prior knowledge (C6-C7, C10-C15) with appropriate citations. The characterization of C. elegans natural habitat (C16-C18) and O2 sensing (C19-C21) is well-supported by literature. The identification of a knowledge gap (C22) appropriately motivates the study. All claims are either properly cited or represent established knowledge.

results.result: C. elegans locomotion occurs via undulatory crawling movements, with body posture tightly coupled to muscle activity and serving as a reliable proxy for motor patterns. Biomechanical principles indicate that both bending amplitude and frequency contribute to locomotion speed.
results.evaluation: These methodological foundations are well-established in the literature with appropriate citations (C8-C9, C43). The relationship between posture and muscle activity (C9) justifies the use of posture analysis as a readout of motor control. The biomechanical principles (C43) provide theoretical support for the observed relationships between undulation parameters and speed.

results.result: Prior literature reported that flp-1 mutants exhibit elevated body curvature and locomotion speed, while NLP-12 neuropeptides are exclusively released from DVA and interfering with DVA/NLP-12 leads to decreased body curvature and locomotion speed.
results.evaluation: These claims accurately summarize prior literature with appropriate citations (C62-C64). The authors successfully replicate these findings in their experimental paradigm (C65), validating the prior work and establishing the foundation for their mechanistic investigations.

results.result: The DVA/NLP-12 and AVK/FLP-1 systems both control locomotion speed in addition to their effects on body posture.
results.evaluation: This is supported by speed measurements across genotypes shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 (C74). The speed phenotypes are consistent with the activity correlations observed in calcium imaging (C83, C87) and provide additional functional validation of the neural systems.

results.result: The postures exhibited by mutant and manipulated strains largely reflect postures that wild-type animals exhibit, though with different frequencies, as shown by 2D density distributions of undulation vs turning amplitude.
results.evaluation: This is demonstrated by the 2D density analysis showing that >90% of mutant postures fall within the 99% boundary of wild-type posture space (C71, Figure 5—figure supplement 1). This important control indicates that the genetic manipulations shift the probability distribution of naturally occurring postures rather than creating entirely novel postures, supporting the interpretation that the neuropeptide systems modulate rather than generate motor patterns.

results.result: flp-1 single mutants and AVK-ablated animals show a stronger tendency to accumulate in the center of the assay arena during control experiments, potentially confounding interpretation of chemotaxis results.
results.evaluation: This observation (C112) is appropriately noted and leads to the justified decision to focus detailed chemotaxis analysis on double mutants and nlp-12 single mutants. This demonstrates good experimental practice in recognizing and addressing potential confounds. The authors speculate this may relate to crowding behavior, though this remains untested.

results.result: Fine-tuned control of undulation and turning motions is essential for normal spatial gradient navigation, though the biased random walk strategy can partially compensate for deficits. In bacteria, biased random walk is the only reported chemotaxis mechanism.
results.evaluation: The requirement for fine-tuned control is demonstrated by the chemotaxis defects in mutants (C109-C110, C113, C115), while the partial compensation by biased random walk is evidenced by retained reversal modulation (C114) and residual chemotaxis ability (C110). The comparison to bacteria (C120) appropriately contextualizes the findings, highlighting the additional complexity of C. elegans navigation.

results.result: Analogous control schemes may govern locomotion in higher animals.
results.evaluation: This is explicitly stated as speculation (C127) without supporting evidence from other organisms. While the general principle of coordinating elementary motor patterns is plausible and the authors appropriately frame this as speculation, no data are provided to support this claim. This represents a reasonable hypothesis for future work but cannot be evaluated as supported or unsupported based on the current study.
